pos: noun (the death of Christ on the cross)
etymology: From the Latin crucifixio, from crux (cross) and figere (to fasten); the Roman manner of execution by which the Lord Jesus was put to death for sinners.
biblical_def: The crucifixion is the central event of redemption, the death of the Lord Jesus Christ upon the cross at Calvary, where He bore the sins of His people and the wrath of God in their stead. Crucifixion was the cruelest and most shameful of Roman executions, reserved for slaves and rebels, and the law of God pronounced a curse upon every one that hangeth on a tree. It was precisely this curse that Christ took upon Himself: He was made a curse for us, redeeming us from the curse of the law. The cross is not a tragedy that befell a good man but the appointed sacrifice in which the just suffered for the unjust to bring us to God. There the handwriting of ordinances that was against us was blotted out and nailed to His cross; there He His own self bare our sins in His own body on the tree; there the penalty due to His people was exhausted, that they being dead to sin might live unto righteousness. The dictionary holds the crucifixion as substitutionary and penal: Christ did not merely display love or set an example, but actually satisfied divine justice by dying in the room of sinners. The preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish, but to the saved it is the power of God; and the believer glories in nothing save the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world is crucified to him and he unto the world.
webster_summary: The death of Christ on the cross at Calvary, the substitutionary and penal sacrifice in which He bore the sins of His people and the curse of the law; the central event of redemption and the power of God to them that are saved.
webster_full: CRUCIFIXION, noun. [Latin crux, cross, and figere, to fasten.] The Roman execution by fastening to a cross; chiefly, the death of Christ.
The cruelest and most shameful of executions, under which the law pronounced a curse (Galatians 3:13).
Christ was made a curse for us, bearing our sins in His own body on the tree.
There the handwriting of ordinances against us was nailed to His cross (Colossians 2:14).
Substitutionary and penal: the just suffered for the unjust, to bring us to God.
scriptures: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
Col 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
corruption_summary: Modern theology empties the cross of its penal substitution, recasting it as mere example, divine solidarity, or—at its worst—“cosmic child abuse,” thus denying the satisfaction of justice that is the heart of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: A wide stream of modern and progressive theology rejects penal substitution, the doctrine that Christ bore the punishment due to sinners. Some reduce the cross to a moral example of self-giving love (the so-called moral-influence theory); others to God's identification with human suffering; and some openly denounce substitution as “divine child abuse.” The dictionary names these as corruptions of the gospel. Scripture is explicit: the LORD laid on Him the iniquity of us all; He was made a curse for us; He bare our sins in His own body. To deny the penal substitution is to deny the very thing that saves.

Equally to be rejected is the Roman recasting of the cross into a sacrifice perpetually re-presented in the Mass. The crucifixion was once for all: Christ once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust; by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). The dictionary holds the finished, sufficient, substitutionary death of Christ as the unrepeatable ground of salvation, and warns that every theory which softens the wrath borne or the justice satisfied leaves the sinner still under the curse the cross alone removes.
roots_summary: From the Latin crux (cross) and figere (to fasten); the Greek stauroo (to crucify) and stauros (cross, stake) name the instrument the gospel turns into the throne of redemption.
roots_lines: Crux, Latin, a cross or gallows; figere, to fasten or fix.
Stauroo, Greek, to crucify; stauros, the cross or upright stake.
The law's curse on “every one that hangeth on a tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23) is taken up in Galatians 3:13.
Anti and huper, Greek prepositions (“instead of,” “on behalf of”), carry the substitution.
Hilasmos, propitiation, names the wrath-bearing accomplished at the cross.
usage: The pastor preached the crucifixion as penal substitution, that Christ bore the wrath due to His people in their stead.
He refused every theory that made the cross a mere example, for Scripture says the LORD laid on Him our iniquity.
She gloried in nothing save the cross, by which the world was crucified to her and she to the world.

etymology: From the Latin humiliatio, a making low, from humus, the ground; the estate in which the Son of God lowered Himself for our salvation, as the catechisms confess.
biblical_def: The humiliation of Christ is the first of His two estates as Mediator, the condition of lowliness into which the eternal Son descended for the salvation of His people, answered afterward by His estate of exaltation. The Shorter Catechism summarizes it: Christ's humiliation consisted in His being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time. The apostle traces its descent: though He was in the form of God, He made Himself of no reputation, took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor, that we through His poverty might be rich. Isaiah foresaw the depth of it: despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. The dictionary holds the humiliation as real and voluntary: the Son did not lay aside His deity but veiled His glory and took our nature with all its sinless weaknesses, descending step by step from the manger to the grave. The estate is the measure of His love and the ground of His sympathy, for the Mediator who saves us first stooped beneath us, that He might lift us to where He now reigns.
webster_summary: The first estate of Christ the Mediator—His descent into lowliness through incarnation, a low birth, the miseries of life, the wrath of God, the cursed death of the cross, burial, and continuing under death—answered by His exaltation.
webster_full: HUMILIATION OF CHRIST, noun phrase. [Latin humiliatio, a making low.] The estate of lowliness into which the Son of God descended to save His people.
It included His being born in a low condition and made under the law.
It included the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross.
It included His burial and His continuing under the power of death for a time.
It was voluntary and real: He made Himself of no reputation and humbled Himself (Philippians 2:7-8).
scriptures: Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Php 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
corruption_summary: The kenotic error supposes the Son emptied Himself of deity in His humiliation, and the prosperity gospel inverts the whole estate, despising the lowliness God exalts.
corruption_paragraphs: A persistent error reads “made himself of no reputation” (literally “emptied himself”) as though the Son laid aside His divine attributes or even His deity in becoming man. The dictionary, with the catholic creeds and the Reformed confessions, rejects this kenotic theology. The Son emptied Himself not by subtraction of His Godhead but by the addition of our nature and the veiling of His glory; He remained fully God while becoming truly man. To suppose otherwise is to deny the immutability of God and to leave us with a Saviour who is less than divine at the very point we need Him most.

The prosperity gospel commits the opposite corruption, despising the whole estate of humiliation. It preaches a Christ of wealth and ease and bids His people seek the same, when the Lord Himself, being rich, became poor for our sakes, and entered glory only through the door of suffering and the cross. The dictionary recovers the pattern the apostle sets: the mind that was in Christ Jesus, who humbled Himself before He was exalted, so that the servant is not above his Lord, and the road to glory still runs through lowliness, obedience, and the cross.
roots_summary: From the Latin humilis (low, lowly), from humus (the ground); the Greek etapeinosen heauton (“he humbled himself,” Philippians 2:8) and ekenosen (“made of no reputation”) frame the estate.
roots_lines: Humilis, Latin, low or lowly, from humus, the earth or ground.
Tapeinoo, Greek, to make low or humble, of Christ humbling Himself unto death.
Kenoo, Greek, to empty, “made himself of no reputation” (by addition and veiling, not subtraction of deity).
Morphe doulou, Greek, “the form of a servant,” the nature He truly assumed.
The catechetical pairing of humiliation with exaltation orders the two estates of the Mediator.
usage: The teacher set the humiliation of Christ against the prosperity gospel, for the Lord became poor to make us rich.
He guarded the catechism's words, that the Son emptied Himself by taking our nature, not by laying down His deity.
She meditated on the descent from the form of God to the death of the cross, and worshipped the love that stooped so low.

pos: noun phrase (the disposition of the Saviour)
etymology: From the biblical use of “heart” for the seat of disposition and affection; the settled disposition of the Lord Jesus toward sinners and saints, revealed chiefly in His own word, “meek and lowly in heart.”
biblical_def: The heart of Christ is the settled disposition and affection of the Lord Jesus toward sinners who come to Him, revealed supremely in His own self-description: “I am meek and lowly in heart.” It is the one place in the Gospels where the Lord lifts the veil upon His inmost disposition, and what He shows is not severity but gentleness toward the weary and heavy laden. The Gospels display this heart at every turn: He was moved with compassion on the multitudes, for they fainted and were scattered as sheep having no shepherd; He wept at the grave of Lazarus and over Jerusalem; He received sinners and ate with them. As a great High Priest He is touched with the feeling of our infirmities, having been tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin, so that He is no distant deity but a sympathizing Saviour who knows our frame. Having loved His own which were in the world, He loved them unto the end. The dictionary marks the heart of Christ against a doubled error: the legalism that pictures a grudging Saviour who must be coaxed to mercy, and the sentimentality that makes His love an indulgent permissiveness blind to sin. The true heart of Christ is gentle and lowly toward the broken, fierce against hypocrisy, holy in all its tenderness; He casts out none that come, yet calls all who come to repentance, and His compassion is the very compassion of God toward His own.
webster_summary: The settled disposition of the Lord Jesus toward sinners—“meek and lowly in heart”—displayed in His compassion, His sympathy as High Priest, and His love unto the end; gentle toward the broken yet holy in all its tenderness.
webster_full: HEART OF CHRIST, noun phrase. The inmost disposition and affection of the Lord Jesus toward His people.
Revealed in His own word: “I am meek and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).
Displayed in His compassion on the shepherdless multitudes (Matthew 9:36).
As High Priest, touched with the feeling of our infirmities (Hebrews 4:15).
Gentle toward the broken, fierce against hypocrisy, holy in all its tenderness.
scriptures: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Heb 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Joh 13:1

Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
corruption_summary: The legalist makes Christ's heart grudging and severe; the sentimentalist makes it an indulgent permissiveness blind to sin—both lose the gentle, holy compassion the Gospels reveal.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption pictures a reluctant Saviour, His heart a closed fist that must be pried open by tears and merit, as though the Father were eager to save but the Son must be persuaded. Scripture overturns this: the Son says of Himself that He is meek and lowly in heart, and that he that cometh to Him He will in no wise cast out. The dictionary recovers the truth that the gentleness of Christ is not earned but freely given, the very disposition of His being toward sinners who come.

The opposite and more fashionable corruption melts the heart of Christ into mere sentiment—an affirming, indulgent love that overlooks sin and asks nothing of repentance. But the same Lord who was moved with compassion drove the money-changers from the temple, denounced the hypocrites with woes, and called sinners to forsake their sin. His tenderness is holy: He receives the broken and the penitent, not the proud and the impenitent. The dictionary holds both together—a heart genuinely gentle toward the weary and heavy laden, and genuinely holy, that loves sinners too much to leave them in their sin.
roots_summary: From the biblical leb (Hebrew) and kardia (Greek), the heart as the seat of thought, will, and affection; Christ's “lowly in heart” (Greek tapeinos te kardia) names His inmost disposition.
roots_lines: Kardia, Greek, the heart as the centre of disposition, will, and affection.
Tapeinos, Greek, lowly or humble, joined to “heart” in Matthew 11:29.
Splanchnizomai, Greek, “moved with compassion,” literally yearning in the inward parts.
Sumpatheo, Greek, to be touched with feeling, of the sympathizing High Priest (Hebrews 4:15).
Eis telos, Greek, “unto the end,” the constancy of His love (John 13:1).
usage: The pastor preached the heart of Christ to weary believers, that the Saviour is meek and lowly and casts out none who come.
He warned against a sentimental Jesus, for the same gentle heart drove the traffickers from His Father's house.
She drew near with boldness, knowing the High Priest is touched with the feeling of her infirmities.

pos: noun phrase (the Spirit's unction of the Messiah)
etymology: From “anoint,” through Old French enoint, from Latin inunctus; the title “Christ” (Greek Christos, “Anointed”) renders the Hebrew Mashiach, Messiah.
biblical_def: The anointing of Christ is the consecration of the Lord Jesus by the Holy Ghost for His threefold office as Prophet, Priest, and King. The very name “Christ” (Greek Christos) and “Messiah” (Hebrew Mashiach) mean “the Anointed One,” for under the old covenant prophets, priests, and kings were set apart by the pouring of oil, a sign of the Spirit's equipping. What the oil signified, the Spirit Himself accomplished in Christ without measure. At His baptism the Spirit descended upon Him, and He opened His ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth by reading Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor.” Peter declares that God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power, and He went about doing good and healing all that were oppressed of the devil. The Psalm sings that God hath anointed Him with the oil of gladness above His fellows. The dictionary holds that this anointing equipped the incarnate Son in His human nature for His mediatorial work—to teach as the great Prophet, to offer Himself and intercede as the great High Priest, and to rule and subdue as the great King. From His fulness His people receive their anointing, for those who are in Christ are made, in their measure, prophets, priests, and kings to God, sharing by the same Spirit in the unction of their Head.
webster_summary: The consecration of the Lord Jesus by the Holy Ghost for His threefold office of Prophet, Priest, and King; the name “Christ” itself means “the Anointed,” and from His fulness His people receive their anointing.
webster_full: ANOINTING OF CHRIST, noun phrase. The Spirit's consecration of the Lord Jesus for His mediatorial office.
“Christ” (Greek Christos) and “Messiah” (Hebrew Mashiach) both mean “the Anointed One.”
God anointed Him with the Holy Ghost and with power (Acts 10:38).
It equipped Him as Prophet to teach, Priest to offer and intercede, and King to rule.
From His fulness His people receive their anointing by the same Spirit.
scriptures: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.
Isa 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
corruption_summary: The charismatic counterfeit detaches “the anointing” from Christ and His office and turns it into a transferable power or aura claimed by self-styled apostles and healers.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern charismatic and word-of-faith teaching has made “the anointing” a free-floating commodity—a power, an aura, a mantle that gifted men possess and impart, often for gain. The dictionary names this as a corruption of the biblical doctrine. The anointing in Scripture is first and supremely the consecration of Christ for His office by the Spirit; what believers receive is a share in His unction, the indwelling Spirit who teaches and seals them, not a transferable energy to be claimed, marketed, or manipulated. The New Apostolic Reformation's talk of “the anointing” severed from Christ's mediatorial work is a counterfeit.

The recovery is the threefold office. Christ was anointed Prophet, Priest, and King, and His people, united to Him, share in that anointing in their measure: they know the truth by His prophetic teaching, they draw near to God by His priestly sacrifice, and they reign over sin by His kingly power (Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 32). The believer's anointing is the indwelling Spirit applying the benefits of Christ, not a badge of spiritual celebrity. The dictionary roots all true anointing in the Anointed One and rebukes every detached and mercenary counterfeit.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew mashach (to anoint) and its noun Mashiach (Messiah), rendered in Greek by chrio (to anoint) and Christos (Christ); both name the Spirit-consecrated One.
roots_lines: Mashach, Hebrew, to anoint or smear with oil, the rite of setting apart to office.
Mashiach, Hebrew, “Anointed One,” whence “Messiah.”
Chrio, Greek, to anoint; Christos, “the Anointed,” whence “Christ.”
The anointing oil of the old covenant figured the Spirit's equipping for office.
Chrisma, Greek, the “unction” believers have from the Holy One (1 John 2:20).
usage: The teacher showed that “Christ” means “the Anointed,” consecrated by the Spirit as Prophet, Priest, and King.
He rebuked the notion of a transferable “anointing,” for the believer's unction is a share in Christ's.
She rejoiced that, being in the Anointed, she too was made by the Spirit a prophet, priest, and king to God.

etymology: From the Lord's own teaching that the Hebrew Scriptures testify of Him; the principle that Christ is the substance and scope of the whole Old Testament.
biblical_def: “Christ in the Old Testament” names the principle, taught by the Lord Jesus Himself, that the whole of the Hebrew Scriptures testifies of Him and finds its fulfilment in Him. On the road to Emmaus, beginning at Moses and all the prophets, He expounded unto His disciples in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself; and He said plainly, “Had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.” He taught that all things must be fulfilled which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning Him. Peter writes that the Spirit of Christ in the prophets testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow. The Old Testament reveals Him in many modes: by direct prophecy (the seed of the woman, the Son of David, the suffering Servant, Immanuel); by type and figure (Adam, Isaac, Joseph, Moses, the passover lamb, the brazen serpent, the tabernacle and its sacrifices, Jonah); by the appearances of the Angel of the LORD; and by the unfolding of the one covenant of grace. The dictionary holds this Christ-centred reading as apostolic, against two errors: the rationalist exegesis that finds in the Old Testament only ancient Israelite religion and denies its witness to Christ, and the undisciplined allegorism that finds Christ in fanciful places the text never warrants. The sound rule is that of the apostles: Christ is the true scope of the Scriptures, read by attention to promise, type, and the analogy of faith.
webster_summary: The principle, taught by Christ Himself, that the whole Old Testament testifies of Him—by prophecy, type, and the covenant of grace—and finds its fulfilment in Him; the apostolic, Christ-centred way of reading the Scriptures.
webster_full: CHRIST IN THE OLD TESTAMENT, noun phrase. The truth that the Hebrew Scriptures testify of Christ and are fulfilled in Him.
On the Emmaus road He expounded in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself (Luke 24:27).
“Had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me” (John 5:46).
He is revealed by prophecy, by type and figure, by the Angel of the LORD, and by the covenant of grace.
The Spirit of Christ in the prophets foretold His sufferings and glory (1 Peter 1:11).
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Joh 5:46
For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.

And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
corruption_summary: Historical-critical exegesis denies that the Old Testament witnesses to Christ at all, while undisciplined allegory finds Him in fanciful places the text never warrants; both depart from the apostolic rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic method treats the Old Testament as the religious deposit of ancient Israel and denies it any genuine forward witness to Christ, dismissing the apostolic readings as later Christian impositions. The dictionary rejects this on the authority of the Lord, who said Moses wrote of Him, and of the apostles, who preached Christ from the law and the prophets. To deny Christ in the Old Testament is to set oneself against the very hermeneutic Jesus taught His disciples after the resurrection, and to make the Spirit of Christ in the prophets a fiction.

The opposite danger is an undisciplined allegorism that finds Christ in every detail by fancy rather than by warrant—the scarlet thread, the colour of a curtain, a number in a genealogy—straining the text past what the apostolic example sanctions. The dictionary commends the sober Reformed practice: read the Old Testament for its genuine prophecies, its God-given types fulfilled in Christ, and its place in the one covenant of grace, governed by the analogy of faith and the New Testament's own interpretation. Christ is truly there, as the substance and scope of all; He need not be smuggled in where the Spirit has not placed Him.
roots_summary: From the Lord's teaching that the law, the prophets, and the psalms speak of Him; the Reformed term “scope” (the central aim of Scripture) names Christ as the substance of both Testaments.
roots_lines: Diermeneuo, Greek, “he expounded” (Luke 24:27), the Lord interpreting the Scriptures of Himself.
Typos, Greek, a type or pattern, the God-given figures fulfilled in Christ.
“The Spirit of Christ” in the prophets (1 Peter 1:11) authors the Old Testament witness.
The Reformed “scope of Scripture” names Christ as the central aim of the whole canon.
The “analogy of faith” governs interpretation, that Scripture expound Scripture.
usage: The preacher expounded the passover lamb as a true type of Christ, following the apostolic rule.
He warned the students against an allegory that finds Christ where the Spirit never placed Him.
She read the Old Testament for the Saviour of whom Moses wrote, beginning at Moses and all the prophets.

pos: noun phrase (the doctrine of imputation in the cross)
etymology: A Reformation phrase (Luther's admirabile commercium, “wonderful exchange”) for the double imputation at the cross: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us.
biblical_def: The great exchange is the Reformation name for the wonderful transaction at the cross in which our sin was reckoned to Christ and His righteousness reckoned to us. The apostle states it in a single verse of unfathomable depth: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” Here is a double imputation. Our sins were laid upon the sinless Christ—the LORD laid on Him the iniquity of us all—and He bore them as our substitute, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God. And the perfect righteousness of Christ, His whole active and passive obedience, is credited to the believing sinner, so that by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Nothing of our own merit enters the transaction; it is reckoning, not infusion—a change of standing before God, received by faith alone. Luther called it the admirabile commercium, the wonderful exchange: Christ takes what is ours (sin, guilt, condemnation, death) and gives us what is His (righteousness, sonship, acceptance, life). The dictionary holds the great exchange as the very marrow of justification: the sinner stands before God not in his own filthy rags but clothed in the righteousness of Another, accepted in the Beloved. To deny the imputation of Christ's righteousness, as Rome and some modern revisionists do, is to leave the sinner naked; to confess it is to glory in a salvation wholly of grace.
webster_summary: The Reformation doctrine of the double imputation at the cross—our sin reckoned to the sinless Christ, His righteousness reckoned to us (2 Corinthians 5:21); the marrow of justification, received by faith alone.
webster_full: GREAT EXCHANGE, noun phrase. [Luther's admirabile commercium, the wonderful exchange.] The double imputation at the cross.
Our sin was reckoned to Christ: He was made sin for us who knew no sin.
His righteousness is reckoned to us: that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him.
It is imputation, a change of standing, not infusion of an inherent quality.
Received by faith alone; the marrow of the doctrine of justification.
scriptures: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:
Isa 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
corruption_summary: Rome and the “new perspective” deny the imputation of Christ's righteousness, recasting justification as infused grace or covenant membership and leaving the sinner without the borrowed righteousness Scripture credits.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman doctrine denies that the believer is justified by an imputed (reckoned) righteousness, teaching instead an infused righteousness that makes him inherently just by degrees, so that justification and sanctification are confused and assurance is lost. The dictionary rejects this on the plain word that we are made the righteousness of God in him—a righteousness that is His and credited to us, not ours by infusion. The great exchange is reckoning: Christ counted a sinner though He had no sin, we counted righteous though we have none of our own.

A subtler modern denial comes from the “new perspective” and allied revisionists, who recast justification as mere covenant membership or future vindication and deny that Christ's active obedience is imputed to the believer. This too the dictionary refuses. Romans 5:19 is explicit: by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. The whole obedience of Christ—His perfect keeping of the law and His penal death—is the righteousness reckoned to faith. Strip away the imputation and the sinner is left in his rags; confess it and he stands accepted in the Beloved, clothed in a righteousness not his own.
roots_summary: From Luther's admirabile commercium (wonderful exchange); the doctrine rests on the Greek logizomai (to reckon, impute) and the “for us” (huper hemon) of substitution.
roots_lines: Admirabile commercium, Latin, “the wonderful exchange,” Luther's phrase for the cross.
Logizomai, Greek, to reckon, count, or impute, the verb of Romans 4 and 5.
Hamartian epoiesen, Greek, “he made him to be sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Dikaiosune Theou, “the righteousness of God,” the standing credited to the believer.
Huper, Greek, “on behalf of, in the place of,” carrying the substitution.
usage: The pastor preached the great exchange, that Christ took our sin and we receive His righteousness by faith alone.
He answered Rome by showing that we are made the righteousness of God in Christ, a reckoned and not an infused righteousness.
She rested her assurance not in her own rags but in the borrowed righteousness of the great exchange.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Greek to pleroma tou chronou, “the fulness of the time”; the appointed and ripened moment of Christ's coming.
biblical_def: The fulness of time is the appointed and ripened moment, ordained from eternity, at which God sent forth His Son into the world. “When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.” The phrase declares that the incarnation came neither too soon nor too late but at the exact hour set by the providence of God, when all things were ready. The dictionary marks the manifold ways in which the time was full: the types and prophecies of the old covenant had run their course and ripened toward their substance; the Roman peace and roads opened the world to the spread of the gospel; the Greek tongue gave a common speech for the apostles; the Jewish dispersion and synagogue prepared a hearing among the nations; and the long failure of the law to make men righteous had exposed the need of a Saviour. So the four hundred silent years and all the centuries before were not empty waiting but God ordering the stage. Mark records the Lord's own announcement at His coming: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” The dictionary holds the fulness of time as a witness to the meticulous providence of God over history: He governs the rise and fall of empires, the spread of languages, the ripening of expectation, all to the end that His Son should come at the perfect hour to redeem His people.
webster_summary: The appointed, ripened moment ordained by God at which He sent forth His Son (Galatians 4:4); a witness to the meticulous providence that ordered history so Christ should come at the perfect hour.
webster_full: FULNESS OF TIME, noun phrase. [Greek to pleroma tou chronou.] The appointed, ripened moment of Christ's coming.
“When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4).
The types and prophecies had ripened; the world was prepared by language, roads, and dispersion.
It witnesses to God's meticulous providence over the course of history.
The Lord announced it: “The time is fulfilled… repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15).
scriptures: Ga 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
Ga 4:5
To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
Eph 1:10
That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him:
And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is a deistic or merely sociological reading that credits the timing of Christ's coming to historical accident rather than the providence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is meticulous providence. A common modern habit explains the timing of Christianity's rise by purely sociological causes—Roman roads, Greek language, political stability—as though these were happy accidents that a clever movement exploited. The dictionary affirms the historical means but denies the deism. Paul says God sent forth His Son when the fulness of the time was come; the means were themselves ordered by the God who governs the rise and fall of empires to the precise end of redemption.

The phrase also rebukes the impatience of the human heart, which questions why God delayed so long or acts so slowly still. The fulness of time teaches that God's appointments are never early and never late; the centuries of promise, the silent years, the long exposure of the law's inability to justify—all ripened the hour. The same providence that timed the first advent governs the second, so the believer waits in patience, knowing the kingdom comes, and shall be consummated, at the hour the Father has set.
roots_summary: From the Greek pleroma (fulness, that which fills) and chronos (time); the time was “full” as a vessel filled to the appointed measure.
roots_lines: Pleroma, Greek, fulness, completion, that which fills up.
Chronos, Greek, time as duration, the appointed span now run out.
Kairos, Greek, the fitting or opportune moment, kin to the idea of ripeness.
The “dispensation of the fulness of times” (Ephesians 1:10) sets it in God's ordering of all ages.
“The time is fulfilled” (Mark 1:15, peplerotai ho kairos) is the Lord's own announcement.
usage: The teacher showed that God ordered roads, tongues, and empires to bring His Son in the fulness of time.
He comforted the impatient with the truth that God's appointments are never early and never late.
She saw the four hundred silent years not as empty waiting but as the ripening of the appointed hour.

pos: noun phrase (the steward of the parables)
etymology: From the Authorized Version; the “good and faithful servant” commended by the lord in the parables of stewardship and watchfulness.
biblical_def: The faithful servant is the figure, drawn from our Lord's parables, of the steward who is found at his Master's return doing the work entrusted to him, and who hears the great commendation, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant… enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” In the parable of the talents the faithful servants traded with what they were given and rendered the increase; the wicked servant buried his talent and was cast out. In the parable of the watchful steward the question is asked, “Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?”—and blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he cometh, shall find so doing. The standard is not the size of the gift but the fidelity of the steward: it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much. The dictionary marks the faithful servant against the corruption that measures discipleship by visible greatness or success; the Master commends faithfulness, not bigness, and the servant with two talents hears the same “well done” as the servant with five. The figure also guards against the presumption of the wicked servant who said in his heart, “My lord delayeth his coming,” and turned to self-indulgence. The believer is a steward of time, gifts, gospel, and household, who labours in his Master's absence and watches for His sure return, that he may give account with joy.
webster_summary: The steward of the parables found doing his Master's work at His return, who hears “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21); the standard is fidelity, not greatness, watchfulness, not presumption.
webster_full: FAITHFUL SERVANT, noun phrase. The steward commended at his lord's return for doing the work entrusted to him.
“Well done, thou good and faithful servant… enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Matthew 25:21).
The faithful and wise servant gives the household meat in due season (Matthew 24:45).
It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2).
The standard is fidelity, not greatness; faithfulness in the least, not the size of the gift.
scriptures: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
corruption_summary: The success-driven age measures discipleship by visible greatness and results, missing the Master's standard of fidelity in what is least and watchfulness in His absence.
corruption_paragraphs: Much modern Christianity, shaped by the metrics of business and celebrity, measures a servant of God by the size of his platform, the numbers of his ministry, the visibility of his gifts. The parables overturn this. The servant with two talents heard the very same “well done” as the servant with five, for the Master commends fidelity, not magnitude. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much. The dictionary recovers the standard: a faithful servant is not a great one by the world's reckoning but a true one by his Lord's, found doing the work entrusted to his hand.

The opposite corruption is the presumption of the wicked servant who said, “My lord delayeth his coming,” and gave himself to indulgence and the beating of his fellow-servants. The delay of the Master is no proof of His absence; He will come in a day the servant looketh not for him. The dictionary holds the parable's sober edge: the steward labours in his Lord's absence and watches for His sure return, neither despairing at delay nor presuming upon it, that he may render his account with joy and not with grief.
roots_summary: From the Greek doulos (bondservant) and pistos (faithful, trustworthy); the steward (oikonomos) is the household manager accountable to his lord.
roots_lines: Doulos, Greek, a bondservant or slave, wholly belonging to his master.
Pistos, Greek, faithful, trustworthy, the quality the master commends.
Oikonomos, Greek, a steward or household manager, accountable for what is entrusted.
Eu, doule agathe kai piste, “well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).
The “talents” and the “meat in due season” figure the gifts and duties of stewardship.
usage: The pastor reminded the small congregation that the Master commends faithfulness, not bigness, and the two-talent servant heard the same “well done.”
He warned against the servant who presumed upon his lord's delay and turned to self-indulgence.
She sought to be faithful in the least things, knowing that fidelity there is the proof of fidelity in much.

etymology: From the account of Mary's breaking the alabaster box of precious ointment upon Christ; the principle that true worship offers to God what truly costs.
biblical_def: Costly devotion is the principle, displayed when Mary broke the alabaster box of very precious spikenard upon the Lord, that true worship and love give to God what truly costs the giver. As Jesus sat at meat in Bethany, a woman came with an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious, broke the box, and poured it on His head; the worth of it was three hundred pence, near a labourer's year of wages. Some present murmured that it was waste, but the Lord rebuked them: “Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me… She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.” He set her deed in everlasting honour, that wheresoever the gospel should be preached, this should be told for a memorial of her. The dictionary binds her act to David's confession when he refused to offer to the LORD that which cost him nothing: “I will surely buy it of thee at a price.” Costly devotion is the opposite of the cheap religion that offers God leftovers, spare moments, and what costs no sacrifice. It is not extravagance for its own sake, nor the buying of merit, for salvation is free; it is the overflow of a heart that has received much and counts no offering too precious for the Lord who gave Himself. The dictionary marks it against both the utilitarian spirit that calls all such offering “waste,” and against the false notion that God can be served acceptably by what costs us nothing.
webster_summary: The principle, shown in Mary's breaking the alabaster box upon Christ (Mark 14:3-8), that true worship offers God what truly costs; against both the utilitarian who calls it waste and the cheap religion that gives God leftovers.
webster_full: COSTLY DEVOTION, noun phrase. The giving to God of what truly costs the worshipper, in love and worship.
Mary broke an alabaster box of very precious spikenard and poured it on Christ (Mark 14:3).
Some called it waste; the Lord called it a good work and set it in everlasting memorial.
David refused to offer that which cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:24).
Not the buying of merit, but the overflow of a heart that has received much.
scriptures: And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head.
And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me.
She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.

And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
corruption_summary: The utilitarian spirit dismisses costly worship as “waste,” while cheap religion offers God leftovers; both miss the heart that counts no offering too precious for the Lord who gave Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The utilitarian objection—“this might have been sold and given to the poor”—sounds pious but was rebuked by the Lord Himself. The dictionary does not despise mercy to the poor, which Scripture everywhere commands; it names the corruption that measures every act of worship by its visible usefulness and calls extravagant love toward Christ a waste. Mary's deed was useful for nothing the world could count, yet the Lord called it a good work and gave it an everlasting memorial. There is a devotion poured out on Christ that needs no further justification than that it was offered to Him.

The opposite and commoner corruption is the cheap religion that offers God only what costs nothing—the spare hour, the loose change, the half-hearted service, the worship that demands no sacrifice. David refused to bring the LORD an offering that cost him nothing, and Mary broke a year's wages over the head of her Lord. The dictionary recovers costly devotion not as a buying of merit—salvation is wholly free—but as the natural overflow of a heart that has received the unspeakable gift and therefore counts nothing too precious to pour out on the Giver.
roots_summary: From the account of the alabaster box (Greek alabastron) of spikenard (nardos pistike); the deed is “a good work” (kalon ergon) the Lord commends, bound to David's refusal to offer what costs nothing.
roots_lines: Alabastron, Greek, a flask of alabaster, here broken to pour out its whole contents.
Nardos pistike, Greek, pure or genuine spikenard, a costly aromatic ointment.
Three hundred pence (denaria) was near a year's wages for a labourer.
Kalon ergon, Greek, “a good work,” the Lord's verdict on the deed (Mark 14:6).
David's “that which doth cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24) sets the principle in the law of offering.
usage: The pastor preached the alabaster box to rebuke a religion that gives God leftovers and spare moments.
He recalled David's refusal to offer what cost nothing, and gave his best to the Lord and not his remnants.
She poured out her costly years on Christ, and counted as gain what the world called waste.

pos: noun phrase (a period of Christ's ministry)
etymology: From Perea (Greek Peraia, “the land beyond”), the region east of Jordan; the later phase of Christ's ministry conducted there and on the road toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: The Perean ministry is the name given to the later phase of our Lord's public work, conducted largely in Perea, the region beyond Jordan, after He withdrew from the hostility of Judea and before His final entry into Jerusalem. John records that He went away again beyond Jordan into the place where John at first baptized, and there He abode, and many believed on Him there—a fruitful season among people prepared by the Baptist's earlier preaching. Matthew marks the move: when Jesus had finished His Galilean teaching He departed and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan, and great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them there. Luke frames the long journey of these months as a steadfast progress: He went through the cities and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem, His face set to the cross. Much of the richest teaching of the Gospels belongs to this period—many of the parables of Luke's travel narrative, the teaching on counting the cost, the lost sheep, coin, and son, the rich man and Lazarus, and the raising of Lazarus that hastened the final opposition. The dictionary marks the Perean ministry as a witness to the deliberateness of Christ's passion: He was not overtaken by events but ordered His own steps, ministering and teaching as He moved with set purpose toward the appointed hour at Jerusalem, the Shepherd going before His flock to lay down His life.
webster_summary: The later phase of Christ's ministry, conducted beyond Jordan in Perea and on the road toward Jerusalem (John 10:40-42; Matthew 19:1); a fruitful season of teaching marked by His deliberate progress toward the cross.
webster_full: PEREAN MINISTRY, noun phrase. [Greek Peraia, “the land beyond.”] Christ's later ministry east of Jordan and toward Jerusalem.
He went beyond Jordan to where John first baptized, and many believed on Him (John 10:40-42).
He came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan, and healed the multitudes (Matthew 19:1).
Luke frames the season as a steadfast journey toward Jerusalem (Luke 13:22).
Much rich teaching belongs here, with His face set toward the cross.
scriptures: And went away again beyond Jordan into the place where John at first baptized; and there he abode.
And many believed on him there.
And it came to pass, that when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee, and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan;
And he went through the cities and villages, teaching, and journeying toward Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the critical fragmenting of the Gospels that denies any coherent ministry and the loss of Christ's deliberate march to the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the deliberateness of Christ's passion. Some critical scholarship so fragments the Gospels into isolated units that it denies any coherent course to the Lord's ministry, treating the geographical and chronological frame as later editorial fiction. The dictionary affirms the Gospels' own ordering: the Lord withdrew beyond Jordan, ministered fruitfully there, and journeyed with set face toward Jerusalem and the cross. He was not the victim of circumstance but the willing Shepherd ordering His own steps.

The Perean season also recovers the breadth of Christ's teaching ministry. Far from a single dramatic act, His work unfolded over years and regions, and the months beyond Jordan gave the church some of its most precious parables—the lost sheep, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, the counting of the cost. The dictionary marks this against any reduction of Christ to a mere sacrifice without a ministry of teaching: He came to declare the kingdom and to die for it, and the road to Jerusalem was lined with the words of life as well as the shadow of the cross.
roots_summary: From Perea (Greek Peraia, from peran, “beyond, across”), the region beyond Jordan; the phrase “beyond Jordan” recurs to mark the location of this ministry.
roots_lines: Peran, Greek, “beyond” or “across,” whence Peraia, the land beyond Jordan.
“Beyond Jordan” (Greek peran tou Iordanou) recurs in John and Matthew for the region.
The “place where John at first baptized” ties the season to the Baptist's earlier labours.
Luke's “journeying toward Jerusalem” frames the travel narrative of chapters 9 through 19.
The set “face toward Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51) marks the deliberate march to the cross.
usage: The teacher located the parable of the prodigal son in the Perean ministry, on the road toward Jerusalem.
He showed that Christ ordered His own steps beyond Jordan, no victim of circumstance but the willing Shepherd.
She marked how many believed beyond Jordan, fruit of seed the Baptist had sown years before.
